questions.question: What is the order of the matrix \( A = \begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ 4 \\ -5 \end{bmatrix} \)?
questions.explanation:

So the order of \( A \) is \( 3\times 1 \).

topics.name: Definitions, Order, Equality and Types of Matrices
topics.summary: A matrix is a rectangular arrangement of numbers in rows and columns. If \( A \) has \( m \) rows and \( n \) columns, its order is written \( m\times n \), and its entry in row \( i \), column \( j \) is denoted \( a_{ij} \), so \( A=[a_{ij}]_{m\times n} \). Two matrices are equal only when they have the same order AND every corresponding entry matches \( (a_{ij}=b_{ij}\text{ for all }i,j) \) -- matching entries alone is never enough. Several special types recur throughout this chapter: a row matrix (\( 1\times n \)), a column matrix (\( m\times 1 \)), a square matrix (\( m=n \)), a diagonal matrix (square, off-diagonal entries \( 0 \)), a scalar matrix (diagonal, every diagonal entry equal to the constant \( k \)), the identity matrix \( I \) (scalar, \( k=1 \)), and the zero matrix \( O \) (every entry \( 0 \)). Each type is a stricter special case of the one before it, and mixing up which condition belongs to which type is the most common source of error here.
key_formulas: \( A=[a_{ij}]_{m\times n} \): order is (rows) \( \times \) (columns)
\( A=B \iff \) same order and \( a_{ij}=b_{ij} \) for all \( i,j \)
Row matrix: \( 1\times n \); Column matrix: \( m\times 1 \); Square matrix: \( m\times m \)
Diagonal matrix: square, \( a_{ij}=0 \) for \( i\ne j \)
Scalar matrix: diagonal with \( a_{ii}=k \) for all \( i \); Identity \( I \): scalar with \( k=1 \)
Zero matrix \( O \): every entry \( 0 \), any order
topics.worked_example:
Classify \( A = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 \end{bmatrix} \).

Every off-diagonal entry is \( 0 \), so \( A \) is diagonal.

Both diagonal entries equal the same constant \( k=-3 \), so \( A \) is a scalar matrix.

Since \( k=-3\ne 1 \), \( A \) is not the identity matrix -- just a scalar matrix with \( k=-3 \).
common_mistakes: Stating the order as (columns) \( \times \) (rows) instead of (rows) \( \times \) (columns)
Treating matching entries alone as sufficient for equality, without checking that the orders also match
Calling any diagonal matrix "scalar", without checking that all diagonal entries are actually equal
Assuming every scalar matrix is the identity matrix, forgetting the constant \( k \) could be anything, not just \( 1 \)

topics.name: Matrix Addition, Subtraction and Scalar Multiplication
topics.summary: Addition and subtraction of matrices are defined only when both matrices have exactly the same order, and are carried out entry-wise: \( (A+B)_{ij}=a_{ij}+b_{ij} \), and similarly for subtraction. If the orders differ, the sum or difference is simply not defined -- there is no rule for combining mismatched shapes. Scalar multiplication has no such restriction: for any scalar \( k \) and any matrix \( A \), \( kA=[k\,a_{ij}] \) multiplies every single entry by \( k \), regardless of the matrix's order. These operations combine naturally, so expressions like \( 2A-3B \) are computed by first scaling each matrix and then adding or subtracting entry-wise, always working with matrices of matching order at each step. The two operations that most often go wrong are stopping halfway through a scalar multiplication (scaling only part of the matrix) and attempting to add or subtract matrices whose orders don't actually match.
key_formulas: \( (A+B)_{ij}=a_{ij}+b_{ij} \), defined only when \( A,B \) have the same order
\( (A-B)_{ij}=a_{ij}-b_{ij} \), defined only when \( A,B \) have the same order
\( kA=[k\,a_{ij}] \), defined for any matrix \( A \) and any scalar \( k \), no order restriction
Combined expressions (e.g. \( 2A-3B \)): scale first, then add/subtract entry-wise
topics.worked_example:
If \( A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \) and \( B = \begin{bmatrix} -4 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \), find \( 2A-B \).

First scale: \( 2A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -2 \\ 0 & 6 \end{bmatrix} \).

Then subtract entry-wise: \( 2A-B = \begin{bmatrix} 4-(-4) & -2-2 \\ 0-1 & 6-(-1) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 8 & -4 \\ -1 & 7 \end{bmatrix} \).
common_mistakes: Scaling only some entries of a matrix by \( k \) instead of every entry
Attempting to add or subtract two matrices of different orders as though it were defined
Subtracting in the wrong order, computing \( B-A \) when \( A-B \) was asked
Mixing up the order of operations in a combined expression, e.g. adding before scaling

topics.name: Matrix Multiplication and Its Properties
topics.summary: The product \( AB \) is defined only when the number of columns of \( A \) equals the number of rows of \( B \): if \( A \) is \( m\times n \) and \( B \) is \( n\times p \), then \( AB \) is \( m\times p \), with each entry given by a row-by-column sum, \( (AB)_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}a_{ik}b_{kj} \) -- never an entry-by-entry product. A crucial fact that surprises many students is that matrix multiplication is not commutative in general: \( AB\ne BA \), even when both products happen to be defined and share the same order. Sometimes only one of \( AB \), \( BA \) is even defined at all. Multiplication does combine sensibly with addition and scalar multiplication, and chains of three or more matrices can be multiplied step by step in the given order (e.g. compute \( AB \) first, then multiply by \( C \) to get \( (AB)C \)). The two dominant errors are multiplying corresponding entries together instead of using the row-by-column rule, and assuming \( AB=BA \) without checking.
key_formulas: \( AB \) defined \( \iff \) (columns of \( A \)) \( = \) (rows of \( B \))
If \( A \) is \( m\times n \), \( B \) is \( n\times p \): \( AB \) is \( m\times p \)
\( (AB)_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}a_{ik}b_{kj} \) (row-by-column sum, not entry-wise product)
In general, \( AB\ne BA \) -- matrix multiplication is not commutative
topics.worked_example:
If \( A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \) and \( B = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \), find \( AB \).

\( (AB)_{11}=(1)(2)+(2)(0)=2 \), \( (AB)_{12}=(1)(-1)+(2)(4)=7 \)

\( (AB)_{21}=(3)(2)+(0)(0)=6 \), \( (AB)_{22}=(3)(-1)+(0)(4)=-3 \)

So \( AB = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 7 \\ 6 & -3 \end{bmatrix} \). (Computing \( BA \) the same way gives a different matrix, confirming \( AB\ne BA \) here.)
common_mistakes: Multiplying corresponding entries together (\( a_{ij}b_{ij} \)) instead of using the row-by-column sum
Assuming \( AB=BA \), or silently computing \( BA \) when \( AB \) was asked
Getting the order of the product wrong, e.g. reporting an \( m\times n \) times \( n\times p \) product as \( n\times n \)
Dropping a term from the row-by-column sum when the inner dimension is \( 3 \) or more

topics.name: Transpose of a Matrix and Its Properties
topics.summary: The transpose of a matrix \( A \), written \( A' \) (never \( A^T \) in this course), is obtained by interchanging its rows and columns: \( (A')_{ij}=a_{ji} \). If \( A \) has order \( m\times n \), then \( A' \) has order \( n\times m \). Four identities govern how transposing interacts with the other operations: \( (A')'=A \) (transposing twice returns the original matrix); \( (A+B)'=A'+B' \); \( (kA)'=kA' \); and, most importantly, \( (AB)'=B'A' \) -- the order of multiplication reverses. This last identity is the single most common trap in the whole chapter: it is the direct analogue of the \( \sin^{-1}x \) vs \( \dfrac{1}{\sin x} \) trap from inverse trigonometric functions, and forgetting to reverse the order (writing \( A'B' \) instead of \( B'A' \)) is an extremely common mistake. These identities let you transpose a combined expression either by computing it fully first and then transposing, or by transposing each piece first and combining -- both routes always agree.
key_formulas: \( (A')_{ij}=a_{ji} \); if \( A \) is \( m\times n \), \( A' \) is \( n\times m \)
\( (AB)'=B'A' \) -- the order reverses
topics.worked_example:
If \( A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \), find \( A' \), and if \( B = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \), verify \( (AB)'=B'A' \).

\( A' = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \) (order \( 3\times 2 \)).

Computing \( AB \) then transposing, and separately computing \( B'A' \), gives the same \( 2\times 2 \) result either way -- confirming the order-reversal identity.
common_mistakes: Writing \( (AB)'=A'B' \), forgetting to reverse the order of multiplication
Reporting the order of \( A' \) as the same as \( A \) instead of swapped

topics.name: Symmetric and Skew-Symmetric Matrices
topics.summary: A square matrix \( A \) is symmetric if \( A'=A \), equivalently \( a_{ij}=a_{ji} \) for every \( i,j \); it is skew-symmetric if \( A'=-A \), equivalently \( a_{ij}=-a_{ji} \) for every \( i,j \). Setting \( i=j \) in the skew-symmetric condition gives \( a_{ii}=-a_{ii} \), which forces every diagonal entry to be exactly \( 0 \) -- a fact that must always be checked, not just the off-diagonal pairs. Both definitions require \( A \) to be square in the first place, since \( A' \) has the opposite order to \( A \), and equality of matrices requires matching orders. Every square matrix \( A \) can be split uniquely into a symmetric part and a skew-symmetric part: \( A=\dfrac12(A+A')+\dfrac12(A-A') \), where the first piece is always symmetric and the second is always skew-symmetric. Classifying a matrix requires checking every off-diagonal pair (and, for skew-symmetry, the whole diagonal) -- not just one pair.
key_formulas: Symmetric: \( A'=A \), i.e. \( a_{ij}=a_{ji} \) for all \( i,j \)
Skew-symmetric: \( A'=-A \), i.e. \( a_{ij}=-a_{ji} \) for all \( i,j \)
Skew-symmetric \( \Rightarrow \) every diagonal entry \( a_{ii}=0 \)
Decomposition: \( A=\dfrac12(A+A')+\dfrac12(A-A') \) (symmetric part \( + \) skew-symmetric part)
topics.worked_example:
Express \( A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 5 \\ 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \) as the sum of a symmetric and a skew-symmetric matrix.

\( A' = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 5 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \).

Symmetric part: \( \dfrac12(A+A') = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \).

Skew-symmetric part: \( \dfrac12(A-A') = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \).

Adding the two parts back together recovers \( A \), confirming the decomposition.
common_mistakes: Classifying a matrix by checking only one entry pair instead of every pair
Forgetting that skew-symmetric matrices must have an all-zero diagonal, not just negated off-diagonal pairs
Reporting the symmetric part when the skew-symmetric part was asked for, or vice versa
Forgetting the \( \dfrac12 \) factor when computing either part of the decomposition
